text.p: Israeli soldiers slipped out of their hilltop base in Hebron at dawn on Friday with little fanfare, handing most of the city to Palestinian rule after 30 years of occupation.
A convoy of jeeps left the fortress-like military governor's heaquarters overlooking the town and about 150 PLO policemen moved in to the sound of sirens and firecrackers.

Only a small, rather subdued crowd was on hand to witness the handshake between officers that set the long-delayed redeployment from 80 percent of Hebron in motion. The United States had put intense pressure on both sides to seal the deal and break a logjam in the wider Middle East peace process.
"At 6.10 the authority was turned over to the Palestinian Authority based on the Hebron agreement," said Israel's West Bank army commander, Major-General Gabi Ofir.
"The keys were turned over successfully according to the Hebron deal," he said.
One Palestinian climbed a tall antenna atop the headquarters to raise the Palestinian flag over the building which President Yasser Arafat was expected to visit within a few days.
Few Hebron residents braved the pre-dawn chill to view the handover, the last of seven West Bank transfers under an interim self-rule agreement between Israel and the PLO.
Palestinian Colonel Awni al-Natshe, deputy Hebron commander, said: "Today we will make the life in the city normal."
Blue-uniformed civilian police then fanned out to direct traffic and joint Israel-Palestinian units began patrolling the border between Jewish and Arab areas.
"I am so happy to see them leave. This will give a chance for peace," said Ziad Abu Rajab, an employee of the Hebron municipality watching the handover.
"But my joy is incomplete. They will still be in the downtown area," he said.
Israel will retain about one fifth of the city where some 400 militant Jewish settlers live.
Israel poured troop and police reinforcements into the town to prevent protests by Jewish settlers opposed to the handover.

"It's a sad morning, sad and difficult," said settler spokesman Aharon Domb. "For anyone who was a part, especially in the first years, of the renewal of Jewish settlement in the city of Hebron, it's a very difficult and sad day."

An Israeli general issued orders on Thursday restricting the movements of 18 alleged Jewish militants for up to 10 days. Some came from Hebron where the settlers live in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs. This makes Hebron unique among the seven West Bank towns already handed over to PLO rule.
Five soldiers for each settler will remain to guard the Jews in the fifth of the town that will remain under Israeli control.
"We are not leaving Hebron, we are redeploying in Hebron," Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said.
His remarks were aimed at right-wingers and settlers who staged a cabinet revolt against the withdrawal.
In Jerusalem, Israel's parliament paved the way for the pullback by endorsing the agreement.
The house voted 87-17, with one abstention, to approve the Hebron deal and three further troop redeployments from mainly rural areas of the West Bank.
The accord, clinched after months of acrimonious negotiations, marked the first time a right-wing government had agreed to hand over territory Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East war to PLO rule.

Israel's commander general in Hebron, who for security reasons could only be identified as Brigadier-General Gadi, was asked to say something to mark the historic occasion as he became the last Israeli to leave the headquarters.
"History speaks for itself," he said.
